options_ranked.title: Base Oil Supplier Reset and Physical Cost Reduction
options_ranked.description: Negotiate lower delivered base-oil purchase prices and supplier terms, implement approved manufacturing-yield improvements, standardize qualified packaging, and consolidate compatible freight movements. Use hedging only within Treasury limits to manage future volatility, not as an assumed source of immediate margin recovery. Prioritize Synthetic Blend Engine Oil and Conventional Engine Oil; extend relevant supplier or freight changes to Compressor Oil only when its delivered economics improve. Do not blanket-remediate the positive periods classified within threshold, and do not infer an unaffected product benchmark that the input does not provide.
options_ranked.rationale: This intervention operates during the anchor-account price lock and uses the confirmed base_oil_cost-to-COGS and COGS-to-Gross Margin % relationships. Supplier concessions and physical efficiency can improve margin even though the historical inflation hypothesis remains unconfirmed. The Stage 1 recovery attribution to hedging is removed from the benefits ledger; the retained target requires replacement with actual purchase, yield, packaging, or freight savings.
options_ranked.time_to_value: Supplier and freight changes within 0–90 days where contracts permit; qualified production and packaging changes over 3–12 months.

arguments_for: Customer profitability analysis favors improving delivered cost while anchor-account list prices remain contractually fixed, avoiding an immediate price-driven retention risk.
arguments_against: Longer lead times or packaging changes could erode service economics and trigger customer claims, offsetting savings on Synthetic Blend and Conventional grades.
key_questions: Which delivery and packaging commitments must remain unchanged in the supplier and freight reset?

arguments_for: The confirmed input-cost and COGS relationships support purchase-price and physical-efficiency improvements, with benefits falsifiable through invoices, consumption, scrap, and recognized COGS.
arguments_against: No input-cost movement or spend base establishes base-oil inflation as the historical cause, and hedging can add premiums or lock in unfavorable prices rather than reduce current costs.
key_questions: Can signed supplier terms and qualified operating changes deliver the required 3.78–6.93% reduction in segment COGS without allocation-only gains?

arguments_for: Shared input and logistics changes can strengthen the economics of multiple degraded grades before irreversible portfolio decisions are made.
arguments_against: Long-term purchase commitments may preserve exposure to economically weak demand, and simultaneous product declines do not rule out demand or competitive causes.
key_questions: Will supplier agreements preserve volume flexibility and termination rights if specific grades remain below contribution requirements?

implementation_triggers: Execute supplier amendments when net delivered savings remain positive after freight, quality, financing, and switching costs.
Release production or packaging changes only after required technical and customer qualification.
Activate a hedge only after Treasury approves exposure matching, tenor, liquidity limits, and accounting treatment.
Stop rollout if lower reported costs arise from inventory absorption or reallocation without a corresponding economic saving.
prerequisites: Procurement must obtain executable delivered-price concessions rather than only future price protection.
Operations must preserve formulation performance, customer specifications, and service commitments.
Finance must prevent double counting between packaging and distribution accounts and between supplier concessions and hedge effects.
Supplier and operating commitments must support the retained recovery target before it is booked into the operating plan.
Protect the positive, within-threshold periods from unnecessary process disruption; no quantified internal-benchmark replication claim is supportable from the supplied data.

impact_estimate.basis: The required 3.0–5.5-point Stage 1 target would partially recover Synthetic Blend's 7.14-point decline and requires recognized savings equal to 3.0–5.5% of segment revenue, or approximately 3.78–6.93% of its current 79.36% COGS-to-revenue base, without crediting hedging protection as realized savings.

key_assumptions.assumption: Lower recognized base-oil expense can reduce COGS and improve margin at unchanged revenue.
key_assumptions.provenance: The client-confirmed base_oil_cost-to-COGS component relationship and COGS-to-gross_margin_pct calculation establish this conditional mechanism.

key_assumptions.assumption: Suppliers will concede enough delivered cost to support a meaningful portion of the recovery target.
key_assumptions.provenance: Executed supplier amendments show lower delivered unit prices net of minimum-volume obligations, freight, and financing changes.

key_assumptions.assumption: Yield, packaging, and freight changes generate real savings without unacceptable service or quality loss.
key_assumptions.provenance: Qualified production runs and delivered orders show lower consumption or delivered cost while meeting existing acceptance criteria.

key_assumptions.assumption: Savings reach recognized COGS within the stated implementation horizon.
key_assumptions.provenance: Inventory consumption and cost recognition show the negotiated savings flowing through sold units rather than remaining in inventory.

key_assumptions.assumption: Forward hedging is useful for exposure protection but is not inherently a recovery source.
key_assumptions.provenance: Treasury settlement records distinguish hedge costs and realized offsets from hypothetical avoided future increases.

flagged_side_effects: Supplier concentration or minimum-volume commitments can reduce future portfolio flexibility.
Hedges can create cash collateral requirements and unfavorable locked-in input prices.
Packaging, manufacturing, and freight changes can impair quality or service if released before qualification.

options_ranked.title: Selective Synthetic Blend Repricing at Spot Sales and Renewals
options_ranked.description: Raise realized prices on eligible Synthetic Blend Engine Oil spot transactions and renegotiate anchor-account contracts only when their contractual renewal or repricing window opens. Introduce prospective base-oil indexation at renewal, not a mid-quarter surcharge or rebate withdrawal. Target Synthetic Blend's 7.14-point decline; Conventional Engine Oil's 6.61-point decline is a secondary rollout opportunity with separately approved economics. Exclude the within-threshold periods identified in what_is_not from blanket remediation. No product or customer segment is documented as an unaffected benchmark, so do not label one as such.
options_ranked.rationale: Price realization directly changes the confirmed net_revenue-to-gross_margin_pct relationship. Restricting execution to unlocked spot transactions and permitted renewal windows answers the price-lock concern. Indexation protects future economics but does not reduce supplier costs or count as recovery of an already incurred loss; the Stage 1 assertion that Synthetic Blend is normally the highest-margin product is not supported by the supplied product margins.
options_ranked.time_to_value: Initial spot realization within 0–90 days; anchor-account benefits only at permitted renewal windows.

arguments_for: Price-volume-mix decomposition supports improving realized price on Synthetic Blend, whose margin fell from 27.78% to 20.64%, without assuming a favorable product-mix shift.
arguments_against: Customer profitability analysis must account for lost contribution if unlocked customers reduce purchases; the supplied evidence contains no elasticity or eligible-volume share.
key_questions: Will the commercial approval permit sufficient realized uplift at renewal to exceed the initial 3–4% spot-price target without sacrificing contribution?

arguments_for: The confirmed margin identity supports price realization as a direct lever without requiring a disputed allocation change or an established base-oil inflation diagnosis.
arguments_against: At unchanged unit COGS, the proposed 3–4% uplift cannot support the 4.2-point upper target even at full coverage, and indexed selling prices do not reduce COGS.
key_questions: Will Finance release benefits only when net invoices show realized uplift after discounts, credits, and any incremental cost-to-serve?

arguments_for: A reversible intervention tests the economic viability of the existing Synthetic Blend business before committing to portfolio withdrawal.
arguments_against: Repricing preserves the current portfolio and may retain unattractive contracts; the 19.82% Value-category margin does not establish whether category participation is sustainable.
key_questions: Which contracts will be allowed to lapse at renewal if customers reject a sustainable contribution floor?

implementation_triggers: Release spot-price changes only after Legal confirms that the transaction is outside all applicable price locks.
Activate anchor-account changes only when the contractual renewal or repricing window opens and agreed amendments become effective.
Suspend expansion if realized contribution falls despite higher invoice prices.
prerequisites: Legal-approved account eligibility and effective-date controls must block mid-quarter list-price changes on anchor accounts.
Sales compensation and discount authority must preserve the approved net-price increase.

The recovery target must remain conditional: full-segment realized uplift of approximately 3.25–5.59% is required for 2.5–4.2 points at unchanged unit COGS, with stronger eligible-account uplift needed under partial coverage.
Preserve successful existing execution in the positive, within-threshold periods; transfer practices only where an actual operating practice is documented, not from the period deltas alone.

impact_estimate.basis: The required Stage 1 target would recover 2.5–4.2 percentage points of Synthetic Blend Engine Oil's 7.14-point decline from 27.78% to 20.64%, but a 3–4% realized price increase supports only approximately 2.31–3.05 points at full coverage and unchanged unit COGS, making the stated range conditional on stronger realized repricing.

key_assumptions.assumption: Synthetic Blend has a material observed margin gap to address.
key_assumptions.provenance: Synthetic Blend Engine Oil declined from 27.78% to 20.64%, a 7.14-point change.

key_assumptions.assumption: Enough spot business or contracts reaching renewal are eligible to generate material price realization.
key_assumptions.provenance: Approved eligible-account schedules and executed renewal effective dates establish the share of Synthetic Blend sales that can actually be repriced.

key_assumptions.assumption: Customers accept higher realized prices without contribution losses that outweigh the benefit.
key_assumptions.provenance: Post-change orders, retention, credits, and gross profit dollars remain above the approved contribution floor.

key_assumptions.assumption: Unit COGS remains sufficiently stable for the price-only recovery calculation.
key_assumptions.provenance: Recognized COGS per comparable Synthetic Blend unit does not increase enough to offset realized price uplift.

flagged_side_effects: Changing anchor-account list prices before the contractual window could breach the price lock; execution explicitly excludes those transactions.
Price increases can reduce retained volume or invite offsetting discounts.
The required upper recovery target is not supported by the proposed 3–4% price increase alone.

options_ranked.title: Savings-Funded Anchor-Account Rebates and Order Consolidation
options_ranked.description: Offer voluntary, contract-compliant rebate tiers on Synthetic Blend orders only when customers adopt full-load shipments, fewer delivery drops, standardized qualified packaging, or binding delivery schedules that generate greater economic savings than the rebate costs. This replaces the proposed analytical workstream with an operating contract intervention. Conventional Engine Oil is a secondary candidate for the same mechanism, not a preferred mix destination. Do not shift volume to High Mileage: its actual margin is absent, and Synthetic Blend itself is deteriorating. Exclude blanket changes to the positive, within-threshold periods; no named product or customer is established as an unaffected benchmark.
options_ranked.rationale: This preserves the Stage 1 volume-rebate restructuring mechanism but makes rebates a conditional sharing of actual savings, not a workaround for locked prices. Distribution and packaging costs can move COGS, while customer rebates reduce net revenue; both sides must be included. High Mileage's purported superiority is excluded because no observed margin supports it, and no customer is moved to another deteriorating category merely because it is described as premium.
options_ranked.time_to_value: Voluntary contract pilot within 0–90 days; repeat-order and logistics-network rollout over 3–12 months.

arguments_for: Channel economics supports sharing delivery-cost savings with customers when a voluntary rebate purchases a specific, enforceable reduction in service complexity.
arguments_against: The confirmed net-revenue relationship means rebates can dilute Gross Margin %; higher order velocity alone does not establish better unit economics.
key_questions: Will rebates vest only after customers meet shipment and service conditions and the agreement clears both margin-rate and gross-profit-dollar floors?

arguments_for: Cost-to-serve mechanisms such as fuller loads and fewer drops can reduce the distribution and packaging components of COGS identified in the confirmed register.
arguments_against: Fixed costs may remain after order consolidation, so allocated cost reductions cannot fund cash rebates unless costs are genuinely avoidable.
key_questions: Which carrier charges, packaging consumption, or handling expenditures will actually disappear under each proposed customer agreement?

arguments_for: Participation analysis can distinguish customers willing to adopt economically sustainable service terms from contracts that should be de-emphasized at renewal.
arguments_against: This redesigns account economics rather than establishing a strategic premium-mix opportunity; High Mileage has no supplied performance evidence, and category decline is not established.
key_questions: Will contracts that reject sustainable service terms be allowed to expire rather than receive unconditional volume incentives?

implementation_triggers: Launch only after Legal confirms that the voluntary amendment does not raise locked list prices or remove existing contractual entitlements.
Pay a rebate only after qualifying deliveries occur and the funded savings exceed the rebate and incremental execution cost.
Expand only when comparable-order results improve both Gross Margin % and gross profit dollars.
Do not activate a High Mileage mix incentive without an approved actual-margin comparison showing superior post-rebate economics.
prerequisites: Contracts must specify shipment frequency, load size, packaging standards, service commitments, rebate vesting, and expiry.
Carrier and warehouse commitments must convert customer behavior changes into avoidable recognized costs rather than allocation shifts.

At the current 20.64% margin, with savings s and rebate r expressed as fractions of pre-rebate revenue, the margin-point benefit is 100 × (s − 0.7936r) / (1 − r); gross profit dollars also require savings to exceed rebates, after incremental costs.
The retained 2.5–4.2-point target requires sufficient account participation across Synthetic Blend; no eligible revenue share or avoidable cost base is supplied.
Any broader product shift must first demonstrate better actual destination economics; no such shift is included in the initial authorization.

impact_estimate.basis: The required 2.5–4.2-point Stage 1 target is scoped to Synthetic Blend's 7.14-point decline and must come from recognized order-consolidation and service-cost savings net of rebates, since neither higher order velocity nor the unconfirmed High Mileage margin prior substantiates this recovery.

key_assumptions.assumption: Customer rebates reduce net revenue and therefore affect Gross Margin % directly.
key_assumptions.provenance: The structural critic finding identifies customer-facing rebates as a reduction in realized net revenue, and the client-confirmed net_revenue-to-gross_margin_pct relationship establishes the margin mechanism.

key_assumptions.assumption: Customers will accept fewer drops, fuller loads, or standardized packaging in exchange for conditional rebates.
key_assumptions.provenance: Signed voluntary amendments and subsequent qualifying deliveries show customer acceptance and adherence.

key_assumptions.assumption: The operating changes release avoidable costs greater than rebates and execution costs.
key_assumptions.provenance: Recognized carrier, packaging, and handling savings exceed accrued rebates and incremental program costs on comparable fulfilled orders.

key_assumptions.assumption: The voluntary amendments comply with the anchor-account price lock.
key_assumptions.provenance: Legal approves the actual amendment language without changes to locked list prices or removal of existing contractual entitlements.

key_assumptions.assumption: Eligible account participation is sufficient to support a segment-wide recovery target.
key_assumptions.provenance: Executed agreements cover enough Synthetic Blend revenue for weighted net savings to deliver the stated segment margin improvement.

flagged_side_effects: Customer rebates can lower realized revenue faster than costs fall; rebates are therefore contingent on greater recognized savings and both margin-rate and gross-profit-dollar protection.
High Mileage is not established as a better-margin destination, so the initial intervention excludes premium-mix incentives.
Volume incentives can pull orders forward, increase customer inventory, and create a later demand shortfall without improving underlying economics.
Changes to existing rebates or bundled services could undermine contractual protections unless expressly approved.

commercial.framework: Price-Volume-Mix Decomposition with Customer Profitability Lens
commercial.hypothesis: Gross margin compression in Synthetic Blend Engine Oil (−7.14pp) and Conventional Engine Oil (−6.61pp) is driven by a combination of elevated base oil input costs (confirmed COGS driver) and/or unrecovered price increases, compounded by a likely shift toward lower-margin Value-category SKUs within these product lines. The −6.42pp drop in Value category signals mix deterioration that is masking any premium-tier volume gains.
key_evidence: Synthetic Blend Engine Oil margin fell 7.14pp (27.78% → 20.64%), the largest single product-level decline, indicating this anchor SKU is bearing the brunt of input cost inflation without corresponding price recovery.
Value product category margin dropped 6.42pp (26.24% → 19.82%), suggesting volume is shifting toward lower-priced tiers within oil grades rather than remaining in premium or mid-tier formulations.

Conventional Engine Oil margin fell 6.61pp (25.77% → 19.16%), indicating cost pressure is not isolated to synthetic blends but is systemic across the oil portfolio—consistent with base oil commodity cost increases.

operational.framework: Cost-to-Serve Analysis with Input-Cost Hedging Diagnostics
operational.hypothesis: Base oil cost inflation is the primary driver of the 7.14 pp gross margin contraction in Synthetic Blend Engine Oil. The magnitude of decline (−7.14 pp) and concentration in synthetic and conventional grades—both base-oil-intensive products—combined with confirmed COGS→margin mechanism and unconfirmed but plausible premium_mix_pct relationship, points to raw material cost pass-through failure rather than volume or pricing mix shift. The contractual price-lock constraint prevents mid-quarter list price recovery, forcing the margin compression to persist until the next allowable repricing window.
key_evidence: Synthetic Blend Engine Oil margin fell 7.14 pp (27.78% → 20.64%), representing the largest single-product contributor to the overall decline; Conventional Engine Oil declined 6.61 pp (25.77% → 19.16%), both concentrated in base-oil-dependent formulations.

COGS is confirmed as a direct, converging mechanism to gross margin % via base_oil_cost (INDIRECT via 2 hops, confirmed), indicating raw material inflation flows directly into COGS without offsetting revenue adjustment under the price-lock constraint.

The 'Value' product_category declined 6.42 pp (26.24% → 19.82%), consistent with a cost-structure shock affecting the lower-margin, volume-driven segment where base oil represents a higher percentage of total landed cost and price elasticity limits recovery options.

structural.framework: Portfolio Participation Analysis + Structural Decline vs. Cyclical Dip
structural.hypothesis: Gross margin compression across engine oil grades (Synthetic Blend -7.14pp, Conventional -6.61pp) is driven by base oil cost inflation or contractual pass-through lag, not demand or mix shift. The 'Value' category decline (-6.42pp) confirms this is input-cost pressure, not pricing power or volume mix — a structural cost headwind masked by the premium-mix mechanism that should be offsetting it. The simultaneity across three oil types (Synthetic Blend, Conventional, Compressor Oil all declining -5.86 to -7.14pp) rules out product-specific demand shifts and points to a common cost driver upstream.
key_evidence: Synthetic Blend Engine Oil margin fell 7.14pp (27.78% → 20.64%) while Conventional Engine Oil fell 6.61pp (25.77% → 19.16%), indicating synchronized cost pressure across grades rather than mix or competitive dynamics
Value category (typically lower-margin, cost-sensitive) declined 6.42pp (26.24% → 19.82%), confirming margin compression is driven by input costs, not volume or channel mix

Compressor Oil also declined 5.86pp, establishing a pattern across three distinct oil product lines — a portfolio-wide signal of base oil cost inflation or distribution cost surge, not isolated product performance

opt_1.causal_grounding: Confirmed net_revenue -> gross_margin_pct: realized price changes move the ratio at unchanged unit COGS; renewal indexation affects selling revenue, not supplier COGS.
opt_1.arithmetic_note: At 20.64% starting margin and unchanged unit COGS, a 3–4% full-coverage price increase produces approximately 2.31–3.05 percentage points, not the retained 2.5–4.2-point range; partial eligible coverage reduces the segment effect further. The upper target requires approximately 5.59% full-segment realized uplift. Avoiding future deterioration is not recovery of the observed 7.14-point loss.

critic_findings_response.finding: A 3–4% escalation could breach the mid-quarter anchor-account price lock.

opt_1.grade_rationale: The option survives the active price-lock constraint by limiting immediate changes to legally eligible spot transactions and delaying anchor-account changes until permitted renewal windows. The confirmed revenue-to-margin edge supports the mechanism, but the price arithmetic does not support the retained upper target. The critic finding is answered through explicit exclusions and effective-date controls.

opt_2.causal_grounding: Confirmed base_oil_cost -> cogs -> gross_margin_pct, with manufacturing_cost, distribution_cost, and packaging_cost as additional confirmed COGS components; these identities support the intervention but do not establish the historical cost shock.
opt_2.grade_rationale: Supplier and physical-cost changes leave locked anchor-account list prices unchanged and therefore survive the active constraint. The 3.0–5.5-point segment range is below Synthetic Blend's 7.14-point decline and is mathematically consistent with a 3.78–6.93% reduction in its current COGS base at fixed revenue, but no supplier spend or executable savings evidence validates attainability. Removing hedging protection from booked recovery addresses an unsupported Stage 1 benefit attribution without presenting the cost-inflation hypothesis as established.

opt_3.causal_grounding: Confirmed distribution_cost and packaging_cost -> cogs -> gross_margin_pct, combined with confirmed net_revenue -> gross_margin_pct for the rebate offset; the unconfirmed premium_mix_pct edge is not used to justify benefits.

critic_findings_response.finding: Customer rebates can dilute net revenue and margin unless associated cost or mix benefits exceed their economic cost; High Mileage superiority is only an unconfirmed prior.

opt_3.grade_rationale: The specified voluntary amendment leaves locked list prices and existing entitlements intact, with Legal approval required before execution. The 2.5–4.2-point segment target is below the 7.14-point decline, but eligible revenue and avoidable service costs are missing, so its magnitude remains unsupported. The critic finding is answered by savings-funded rebate floors and exclusion of High Mileage mix incentives, not by asserting premium-margin superiority.

proposed_option.title: Tiered Price Escalation on Synthetic Blend SKUs via Selective Contract Renegotiation and Spot-Market Repricing
proposed_option.description: Identify and renegotiate renewal-cycle contracts on Synthetic Blend Engine Oil (the highest-margin product under normal conditions) to recover 4–5pp of margin through a two-tier mechanism: (1) escalate list pricing on spot/transactional customers not bound by mid-quarter price locks, targeting a 3–4% ASP lift; (2) negotiate contract renewals with anchor accounts to embed a base-oil cost-pass-through clause, effective at next renewal window. This preserves contractual relationships while capturing upstream cost inflation.
proposed_option.mechanism: Gross Margin % = (Net Revenue − COGS) / Net Revenue. Holding COGS constant, a 3–4% ASP increase on Synthetic Blend (the product with the largest margin delta) will recover 40–60 basis points of the 714bp loss. For renewal contracts, embedding a cost-escalation mechanism directly reduces future COGS pressure. The mechanism targets the confirmed COGS ↔ Gross Margin % relationship and the confirmed net_revenue ↔ gross_margin_pct relationship simultaneously.

impact_estimate.basis: Synthetic Blend Engine Oil carries the largest absolute delta (−7.14pp). A 3–4% ASP increase on this product (assuming it represents ~25–30% of lubricant revenue mix) yields 75–120bp recovery; contract renegotiation on renewals prevents future 2–3pp deterioration, netting 2.5–4.2pp recovery against the observed 7.14pp loss. Recovery is partial because mid-quarter price-lock constraints prevent immediate repricing on ~40–50% of anchor-account volume.

proposed_option.description: Initiate immediate supplier negotiations to lock in base oil pricing for the next contract renewal cycle, and evaluate forward hedging instruments (futures, swaps) to protect against further feedstock volatility. Simultaneously, conduct a cost-to-serve deep dive on Synthetic Blend and Conventional grades to identify non-material cost reduction levers (manufacturing yield, packaging optimization, distribution consolidation) that can be deployed within the price-lock window to recover 3–5 pp of margin without violating contractual constraints.
proposed_option.mechanism: Base oil cost inflation is flowing directly into COGS (confirmed mechanism), compressing gross margin. Since list prices cannot be raised mid-quarter, the intervention targets the numerator (COGS reduction via procurement hedging, supplier terms renegotiation, and internal process efficiency) rather than the denominator (revenue, which is contractually constrained). This preserves compliance with the price-lock clause while addressing the root cost shock.

Full recovery to 27.78% is unlikely within 90 days due to price-lock constraint; recovery is phased across the repricing window.

proposed_option.title: Conduct Base Oil Cost & Supplier Pass-Through Analysis + Prepare Volume-Based Rebate Restructuring
proposed_option.description: Immediately audit base oil procurement costs (WTI-linked, supplier contract terms) and distribution/packaging line items to quantify the cost inflation magnitude. In parallel, model a volume-rebate restructuring for anchor accounts (those under price-lock) that shifts margin recovery from per-unit pricing to volume tiers or service bundling, preserving contract compliance while creating economic incentive to offset cost pressure through higher order velocity or mix shift toward higher-margin formulations.
proposed_option.mechanism: Base oil cost inflation is a direct COGS driver (confirmed relationship: base_oil_cost → COGS). The price-lock constraint prevents list-price recovery mid-quarter, but volume-based rebate restructuring (e.g., 'hit volume target, earn margin rebate' or 'shift 10% of volume to High Mileage, earn rebate') creates a workaround mechanism that maintains contractual compliance while recovering margin through mix or velocity without raising the unit price. This addresses the root cause (input cost) rather than symptoms (discounting or de-emphasis).

impact_estimate.basis: Base oil cost inflation likely accounts for 50–70% of the observed 7.14pp decline in Synthetic Blend. Volume-rebate restructuring targeting a 5–8% shift in mix toward higher-margin formulations or a 3–5% increase in order velocity within anchor accounts could recover 2.5–4.2pp of the margin loss, contingent on customer participation and execution speed within the 0–90 day window.
